title: Populorum Progressio (1967)
hook: Paul VI: development is the new name for peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the signs of the times: look closely at events, then read them in the light of the gospel. Your line was read the signs. Which person in the news stayed with you? Day one thousand three hundred four.

Development is the new name for peace. It sounds like a line off a charity poster, or the tagline of an aid agency. It comes from a papal letter. Paul the Sixth wrote it near the end of Populorum Progressio, a letter on the development of peoples. The idea underneath is plain enough to fit in a lunch break. A world where some nations feast while others go hungry is not at peace, however quiet the borders look. If you want peace, the letter says in effect, help people grow. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `A LINE OFF A POSTER?` → `THE DEVELOPMENT OF PEOPLES.` → `NO PEACE BESIDE HUNGER.`

segments.voice: First, what development means here. Paul the Sixth insists it can't be measured by money alone. Real development, he writes, has to promote the good of every person and of the whole person. Food, yes, and health, and work. But also learning, culture, friendship, prayer. Growth that fills the bank and empties the person isn't the thing he means. Second, a hard paragraph about property. The letter says private property is not an absolute right with no conditions on it. No one, it says, may keep for their own exclusive use what they don't need, while others lack what they need to live. And it calls in a voice from the early Church, Saint Ambrose, who told the wealthy, roughly: when you give to the poor, you aren't giving them what's yours. You're handing back what is theirs. Third, nations, not just neighbors. The same logic runs between countries. The letter asks that what rich countries have beyond their needs be put at the service of poorer ones. Generosity isn't left to individuals; it becomes a question for whole peoples. Fourth, peace. Isaiah has a line, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the work of justice shall be peace." Paul the Sixth reads peace the same way. It isn't simply the absence of war. It gets built, day after day, by justice. That's how a letter about wells, schools and fair trade can end by talking about peace.
screen: `EVERY PERSON, AND THE WHOLE PERSON.` · `PROPERTY ISN'T AN ABSOLUTE RIGHT.` · `WHAT RICH NATIONS HAVE TO SPARE.` · then, large: `THE WORK OF JUSTICE SHALL BE PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: support a development cause. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one kind of work that helps people grow on their own terms: a well dug, a girl kept in school, a small loan for a market stall, a clinic open after dark. Don't pick the biggest. Pick the one that moves you. Hold the faces of the people it serves. Then ask what you could give it: money, time, a voice, a share on a feed. If you pray, you can hold that work before God. When the bell rings, make one small note of what you'll do. The bell holds the time.
Populorum Progressio. The development of peoples: Paul the Sixth's letter on the growth of every person and the whole person, and on peace built by justice. Today's word.
Your line: development is peace. Today, follow through on the note you made, even a small gift or five minutes of reading about the work you chose. Day one thousand three hundred four.

howItsDone: Catholics often support development work through parish collections and Catholic aid agencies, and Populorum Progressio is a standard text in Catholic teaching on global poverty and fair trade.
